sections.heading: Arunachal Pradesh- Monument- Malinithan and Bismaknagar
sections.content: Malinithan and Bismaknagar are important archeological sites in Arunachal Pradesh. Malinithan has many granite images of Hindu gods and goddesses. Bismaknagar is situated at the foot of Mishmi Hills in Lohit district. It has a ruined fort that dates back to the period of the Mahabharata. There are also the

sections.heading: Arunachal Pradesh- Monument- Itanagar
sections.content: Itanagar is known to have been built on the ruins of Mayapur, a city that once served as the capital of the eleventh century Jitri dynasty. The rulers of this dynasty built many forts, the most important one being the Ita Fort. Constructed by King Ramchandra, it is the most striking architectural remain of the ancient town. There is a yellow-roofed Buddhist Temple at a hilltop in the town. It is surrounded by beautiful gardens that provide a panoramic view of the temple.

sections.heading: Arunachal Pradesh  Museum - Jawaharlal Nehru Museum
sections.content: Itanagar has the Jawaharlal Nehru Museum which displays extensive collection of local tribal art including wood carvings, musical instruments, textiles, handicrafts and archeological finds. One can understand the socio-cultural heritage and lifestyle of the people of Arunachal Pradesh from the displayed objects in the museum.

sections.heading: Arunachal Pradesh - Handicrafts
sections.content: Arunachal Pradesh is a land of beautiful handicrafts where people have a tradition of artistic craftsmanship. A wide variety of crafts such as weaving, painting, pottery, basketry, woodcarving etc. are found among the people here.

sections.heading: Bamboo Craft
sections.content: The craftsmen of Arunachal Pradesh make various cane and bamboo articles for domestic requirements. Bamboo and cane are found in abundance in this region due to the heavy rainfall and temperate climate. The tribal population uses these materials almost exclusively for constructing their dwellings, utensils, furniture, and even weapons such as bows and arrows, spears, armor, and implements like dibbles, hunting and fishing traps. Bamboo and cane are also transformed into colorful basket mats, cane belts, attractive smoking pipes, combs, and a variety of household tools and

sections.heading: Arunachal Pradesh - Handicrafts - Carpet
sections.content: One of the important creative activity in the district of Tawang, is the weaving of carpets. A speciality of the Monpas, the Buddhist community, is that it is done mainly by women. The weaving is done with exotic designs of dragons, geometric and floral patterns.

sections.heading: Arunachal Pradesh- Handicrafts- Handlooms
sections.content: Weaving is an important household industry involving the women of Arunachal Pradesh. The actual weaving is done with a bamboo tube and using cotton and wool. Bark fibres extracted from trees like udal, pudu and grasscloth is also used. The designs are essentially geometric varying from formal arrangement to lines and bands. The colors that are generally used in the weaves are black, yellow, dark blue, green and scarlet - all put together in the most fascinating combinations. There is an abundant use of natural dyes in the weaving though a lot of synthetic dyes are now used. The Tibetan and Bhutanese influence is evident in the Monpa loom on which the Monpa women weave with cotton, wool and bark fibre. They are well known for their fine and colourful coats, shawls, sashes, carpets, bags and tapes (for tieing around hats). The Apatanis are traditionally the most advanced weavers of the state producing excellent ceremonial coats and shawls, and embroidered cotton cloth.Many tribes such as the Nishis, Hill Miris, Akas, Bugums and Mijis depend on the Apatanis for their supply of cloth. Singpho weaving is famous for its artistic patterns. Similarly, the Tangas are reputed for their spun-dyed clothes out of which they make handbags,

sections.heading: Tangkha painting
sections.content: in one of the most artistic crafts prevalent mainly in Buddhist dominated areas like Tawang, West Kameng and Upper Siang Districts. Thangka refers to the flat cloth on which paintings are produced and by extension to the images and paintings themselves. The motif of the painting is mostly on religious subjects along with traditional values.

sections.heading: Arunachal Pradesh- Handicrafts- Woodcarving
sections.content: Woodcarving has a long tradition among the Monpas, Khamtis, Wanchos, Phom and Konyak tribes. The main center for woodcarving and woodcraft in the state is the Wancho area of Tirap district. The Wancho woodcarvings have three functions. The first is the one connected with headhunting; the second with the decoration of the Morungs or mens communal houses; and the third with the funerary images of different animals. The Wancho wood carver has a deep sense of proportion. In carving of the human figure, special attention is paid to the head. The features are carved in low relief and are fairly realistic. The tribes like Monpas, Sherdukpens, and Bugums create a variety of coloured masks. The masks are made of a single block of wood hollowed inside and holes are usually but not always made for eyes and mouths. Masks are only worn by boys and men. Women never wear

sections.heading: Jewellery
sections.content: made of brass, bone, ivory, silver, and gold are made by many tribes of Arunachal Pradesh. The Monpas are known traditional silversmiths. Brass is skilfully shaped into ornaments, dishes, sacred bells and smoking pipes. The Khamtis work mainly in gold, iron, silver and ivory. The Gallong women wear ear-plugs and earrings. Plugs are generally of leaf, wood or bamboo, while the rings are heavy and coiled and made of iron. The rings are and specially used by the Gallong women. Beads of various colours and sizes, blue feathered wings of birds and green wings of beetles are also used as embellishment.

sections.heading: Arunachal Pradesh- Handicrafts- Pottery
sections.content: Women of the Dafla clan are accomplished potters. Finished pots are not polished or burnished but are carefully kept in the shade for drying. When completely dry, they are put in a fire out-side the house. There are no kilns or pot-ovens. Pottery is used primarily for making cooking utensils.

sections.heading: Dances
sections.content: Dance is an important part of the lives of the people of Arunachal Pradesh, performed on various occasions such as rituals, festivals and also for recreation purposes. They vary from highly stylised religious dance dramas of the Buddhists to the martial steps and colourful performances of the Noctes and Wanchos. Both men and women take part although there are some dances such as Igu dance of the Mishmi priests, war dances of the Adis, Noctes and Wanchos, ritualistic dance of the Buddhist tribes, which are performed only by male dancers. The Monpas, besides performing Monastic dances for three days during Torgya festivals, also perform other dances on different occasions. Some of them are- Aji Lhamu dance, yak dance and lion and peacock dances etc. Some of the popular folk dances of the people are Aji Lhamu (Monpa Tribe), Roppi (Nishing Tribe), Hiirii Khaniing (Apatani Tribe), Popir (Adi Tribe), Pasi Kongki (Adi), Chalo (Nocte Tribe), Ponung (Adi Tribe), Rekham Pada(Nishing Tribe), Lion and Peacock dance (Monpa) and so on. Dances are accompanied by songs sung generally in chorus.

sections.heading: Festival
sections.content: s play an essential role in the socio-cultural life of the people. They are essentially connected with agriculture and celebrated with ritualistic gaiety to thank God or to pray for a bumper harvest. Some of the important festivals are Mopin of Galos, Solung of Adis, Lossar of Monpas, Dree of Apatanis, Si-Donyi of Tagins, Nyokum of Nyishis, Reh of Idu Mishmis etc. Animal sacrifice is a common ritual in most festivals. The 'Solung' is the main festival of Adis. It is celebrated to reap a rich harvest after sowing of seeds and transplantation of paddy plants, to raise more animals and also to be free from natural and other calamities and the prosperity of men. There is singing, dancing and animal sacrifices in this five-day festival. 1600-1650 Medieval Tawang Monastery or Gompa is a 400 year old monastery of the Mahayana sect of the Buddhists. Built in the seventeenth century, at a height of 10,000 ft the monastery was founded by a monk called Mera Lama. It is an enormous complex of 65 buildings - a treasure house of old scriptures, priceless images, painted tapestries, books and collection of gold lettered Buddhist scriptures. The Parkhang hall of the monastery houses the library which holds the rare hand written and block-printed Thangkas or manuscripts of revered books like Tangym, Kangyur and Sungbhum. The other rare works of Buddhist literature include 108 gold-embossed manuscripts of the Teaching of Lord Buddha and 225 volumes of the explanations of Buddhas teachings covered with specially designed moth - proof silk adorned with paintings. There is a towering eighteen feet high gilded statue of the Buddha in the monastery complex. Besides the monastery the town promotes the small-scale industries and local handicrafts at their Handicrafts Centre, which has a fine range of woollen carpets and shawls amongst other crafts. The Tawang Monastery is associated with the famous Torgva festival which is held in the eleventh Monpa month called the Dawa Chukchipah
